in writing. − the continuing decline of traditional industries means that many regions in the european union need support to cope with the conversion and restructuring of their former industrial areas. the commission is therefore proposing to increase the use of the cohesion fund. of course, the individual regions need financial support. however, i think it would be more sensible - particularly in view of the billions of eu grants that end up in the dark channels and in the black boxes every year - to regulate such grants at national level in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity. finally, it is the same countries which are repeatedly singled out in the court of auditors' report for fraud and for which the recovery of funds wrongly paid does not work properly. i cannot therefore support this report.
in writing. − european industry has enormous potential for growth, innovation and employment. although the share of the industrial sector in gdp has declined in recent years, it still stands at 16%. this is why it is important to start locally, support existing industrial areas and promote reindustrialisation through eu funds. i voted for this report because it emphasizes an integrated approach. the commission has also proposed that the community should be able to provide aid to the countries of central and eastern europe in the form of loans for the financing of small and medium-sized enterprises. the importance of innovation and the cultural and creative industries in a reindustrialisation process is also discussed. i know from my own experience that the safeguarding of industrial jobs and the promotion of the creative economy at the same time is to the benefit of all, as exemplified by the city of linz.
in writing. − this report deals with regional strategies for industrial areas in the eu. industry is one of the most important factors for the eu's competitiveness and has always been important for creating jobs and promoting growth and innovation. the eu industrial sector has weakened over the last 50 years (current share 16%) and the development of regional strategies for former industrial areas is necessary. sustainable regeneration of former industrial regions is very costly, so eu public cohesion policy funds must play an important role. the aim is to highlight the characteristics of the regions which are common to all former industrial regions and to identify possible solutions.
in writing. - it makes a huge difference whether you are drilling 2,000 metres below sea level or 7,000 metres below. you're ready to go deeper and deeper. if we want to increase the safety of offshore installations, we also need to think about control. and while we are talking about the safety of offshore oil production sites, we should also be thinking about reducing the environmental impact of the normal operation of oil production and production facilities. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat pollution. the present report contains good approaches to this problem, although not to a sufficient degree. i have adjusted my voting behaviour to this effect.
in writing. − as renewable energies make an important contribution to a more independent and low-emission energy supply in europe, their share needs to be progressively increased. the european leadership in the development of renewable energy technologies should be further developed. however, europe's competitiveness should not be put at a disadvantage. international agreements should be concluded which also commit the usa, china and other industrialized countries to increase the use of renewable energy. the energy transition must also be financially viable for small and medium-sized enterprises. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of renewable energy sources, in particular nuclear power stations, and to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of renewable energy sources. i am not going to go into the details of the amendments, but i would like to say that i am not in favour of the amendments.
in writing. - the rapporteur has dealt with the complex issue of the combination of renewable energy sources and the european internal market in a very nuanced way. it clearly identifies the benefits, explains the challenges and sets ambitious targets for the integration of renewable energy in the internal market. in addition to the positive effects of these objectives, the rapporteur has also taken account of the interests of other areas: for example, it emphasizes food security in parallel with the use of biomass as an energy source, or it explicitly includes the situation of agriculture, which may change significantly as the share of biomass increases. the progressive handling of the infrastructure requirements (e.g. acceleration of energy infrastructure projects, expansion of hydroelectric storage in different countries) makes it impossible to agree with the report as a whole.

i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. i voted for the report. i would like to make a brief criticism of net neutrality. the issue of net neutrality is only mentioned in passing in this report. but much more would be needed. we need to set a new priority list so that we can really do justice to traditional media and new media. why is net neutrality important? what is net neutrality? net neutrality means that we treat all data on the net equally, that we don't favor any data. if we give preference to certain data, we give the big networks the right to influence our content, what we read, what we are informed about. so the issue of net neutrality has a big impact on media freedom, on freedom of expression and also on the right to freedom of information. this is why it is important that we actually enshrine net neutrality in law at european level, rather than just casually affirming and mentioning the principle.

president-in-office of the council. − madam president, i am very pleased to have the opportunity to take part in this afternoon’s debate on the package of regulations establishing the single supervisory mechanism and adapting the set-up of the european banking authority. in may 2012, the commission called for a banking union, to restore confidence in banks and in the euro. this was reflected in the report on economic and monetary union prepared by the presidents of the european council, the commission, the eurogroup and the european central bank. a complete banking union requires common supervision, deposit insurance and a common resolution framework, with an appropriate fiscal backstop. centralising supervision was the first step in this process. therefore, the immediate priority for the proposal was to create a single supervisory mechanism (ssm) for the euro area, with the ecb taking on the prudential supervision of credit institutions. this package of texts, the ecb regulation conferring supervisory tasks on the ecb, and the amended eba regulation will lay the foundations of a new and more effective system of supervision for all the participating member states. the new system will neither do away with nor duplicate the national supervisors, but it will incorporate them into a more powerful architecture centred on the ecb. at the same time it will make full use of the resources and skills of the national authorities. the eba will preserve its role in preparing draft regulations and will see an increase in its powers, particularly regarding the assessment of the resilience of our banking systems. this is a significant achievement, and i will set out some of its key aspects in a moment. it is particularly significant that it has been accomplished in only two and a half months of intense negotiations. i would therefore like to pay particular tribute to the econ chair, sharon bowles, and the two excellent rapporteurs, marianne thyssen and sven giegold, for their dedication and the constructive way they have enabled our two institutions to cooperate. the crisis that has hit our economies in the last five years has revealed considerable weaknesses in many banking systems and in the way they were supervised. billions of euros of public money have been committed to supporting the banking system, whilst budgetary constraints have been imposed on other policies. this has led to very considerable and understandable public frustration. the single supervisory mechanism is a major step forward in restoring the confidence of markets and the public in the strength of our supervisory system. i will briefly mention some of the key provisions of the agreement reached between our institutions. firstly – and importantly – we have agreed on the distribution of work between the ecb and the national competent authorities. we have sought to reconcile the cohesiveness of the supervisory architecture – to have a true single supervisory mechanism – with the need to make the most of national supervisors’ competences and local reach. the ecb will concentrate supervision on the most significant institutions determined on the basis of size, importance to the national economy in home member states, and the extent of its cross-border activities but will also be able to expand its direct supervisory role in the light of identified needs. it will in any case be able from the outset to guide the actions of national supervisors. the ecb will also be able to exercise some macro-prudential powers, in cooperation with national authorities. overall, we have in our negotiations sought, where relevant, to respect the balance of prerogatives between home and host member state supervisors. since the single supervisory mechanism will bring about a major institutional change, it is important that it builds on existing arrangements based on current banking legislation. the powers of the ecb must of course be balanced by adequate accountability and governance arrangements, to which this parliament has made a particularly important contribution. there will also be important safeguards regarding the separation of the supervisory function from the monetary policy function within the ecb. however, it is clear that the governing council remains the key decision-making body of the ecb. the authorities from all participating member states will be represented, alongside the ecb, on the supervisory board in charge of preparing decisions. we have agreed on the establishment of robust safeguards, including the establishment of a mediation panel, to resolve differences of views between member state authorities when the governing council objects to a draft decision. these also relate to the appointment of the chair and vice-chair of the supervisory board, where parliament now has a very prominent role. safeguards were also needed for non-euro area member states willing to participate in the single supervisory mechanism, with the aim of making the new system as attractive as possible to non-euro area member states. these additional safeguards recognise that the non-euro-area member states are not represented in the governing council and cannot fully benefit from the other mechanisms provided for the euro-area member states. the text, i believe, achieves a good balance on this particular issue, and i understand that many countries have given indications that they are considering joining the ssm as a result. the package before us today sends a hugely important signal to markets. when the ecb takes up its full supervisory powers around summer next year, this will constitute a major change to the current system. we will have put in place the first pillar of the banking union. we will have shown that we are together determined to make our financial system more robust. but we should not be complacent. the ssm is of course only the first step on the path to establishing the banking union. together we have a lot more work to do to complete that task, and i know we can count on the continued cooperation of parliament in order to achieve that.
member of the commission. - madam president, hello to each and every one of you. i would also like to thank, first of all, marianne thyssen and sven giegold for their appreciation of our cooperation and the work that the commission has done, quickly and seriously, indeed, throughout the summer of last year, to put on your table, as a collective package - it was a commitment we had made to deal with these two subjects together - and on the part of the ministers, this important piece, major for europe, of integrated supervision, as, by the way, i say, another major piece. the european parliament and the council have recently approved a text which is fundamental to the robustness of the european banking sector, the crd iv directive. this legislative package, ladies and gentlemen, is, as we all know, the first step towards what is known as banking union. the aim of this banking union is to restore confidence in banks and to ensure the soundness and reliability of the banking sector. it must also help to strengthen the internal market, which has been - as sven giegold rightly said - undermined by the financial crisis, and, finally, to guarantee financial stability, which is one of the conditions for a return to confidence and growth. with the creation of the single supervisory mechanism, we are ensuring a common, impartial and european supervision of banks. the transnational banks, which will be in trouble, will no longer be able to be managed at the level of a single member state and its supervisor, without a global approach and without coordination. i am convinced, ladies and gentlemen, that if we had had this single supervisory mechanism earlier, we could have prevented the problems we have encountered in recent years in many banks, in almost all the banking crises in the single market. the national supervisors will of course continue to play the important role of a clear division of labour with the european central bank, but their work will now be part of the single supervisory mechanism and will be placed under the aegis of the european central bank, which will have the responsibility of ensuring the proper functioning of this mechanism, as marianne thyssen has recalled. although the single supervisory mechanism was initially limited to the euro area, we have committed ourselves, as many of you have wished, to ensuring that the integrity of the single market is fully preserved, thanks to the dedicated role of the european banking authority. i now come to a subject which raises questions and, at times, concerns. the specific rules on the governance of the european central bank will ensure a strict separation between supervisory tasks and monetary policy functions. i know that some of you would like to see it go further, but if we look carefully at the regulation we have on the table today, i think that in practice supervision and monetary policy will indeed be completely separate. i would like to thank the presidencies of the council of the european union, in particular the cypriot presidency and, dear linda, the irish presidency, which have been very proactive on this matter, and then, of course, i would like to thank european commission, your two rapporteurs, marianne thyssen and sven giegold, and many of you, including sharon bowles, sylvie goulard, mrs klinz, mrs lamberts, mr sánchez presedo and mr pittella, who have taken part in various meetings of the trilogues, which have been very numerous, and all the other members who have contributed to this constructive discussion. this contribution of parliament has been fundamental in two respects, which you have mentioned in particular: first, the democratic responsibility of the european central bank; second, the need to ensure that the european central bank is not a mere institutional institution. the standards of supervision that your parliament has obtained are among the highest in the european union, and rightly so, because the european central bank will have very important supervisory powers. i very much hope that the specific arrangements to be negotiated in this interinstitutional agreement with the european central bank will allow for the effective implementation of this democratic control. as you both have said, sven giegold and marianne thyssen, this is a question of democracy and i also hope that these arrangements will be approved in that spirit as soon as possible, so that supervision can be effective, operational and rapid, at the beginning of 2014. on the other hand, the voting arrangements within the european banking authority have been adapted so that decisions take full account of the interests of all member states. i very much hope - but it is, of course, for you to decide - that parliament will welcome these texts and be able to give its final approval as soon as possible. i repeat that it is very important, as the european central bank is preparing for this, that this supervisory mechanism should be operational in the first months of 2014. it should of course be stressed that this operational implementation will not be effective, according to the texts before us, until one year after publication in the official journal. thanks to you, ladies and gentlemen, and thanks to the council, a strong signal will be sent to the markets, to our international partners and, first and foremost, to the citizens, who want to learn from the crises that have affected them, that have weakened them, who have called for considerable public contributions - almost 11 or 13 per cent of gdp at the time of the financial crisis - a signal that the european union is firmly committed not only to learning from this crisis but also to stabilising the euro area, strengthening the single market and thus laying the foundations for a resumption of growth. it will also allow us to start working quickly on the establishment of a single resolution mechanism, which is another major part of the banking union and which i intend, on behalf of the commission, to propose to the council of ministers and the european parliament in the coming weeks. in writing. - the worsening economic and euro crisis has certainly led to a deterioration in the situation of social housing. as the report rightly points out, the needs vary between member states. there are also regional variations in the member states (urban and rural areas, urban centres, suburbs, etc.). with regard to the above-mentioned overcrowding of housing, it should be noted that this problem mainly affects immigrants or people with a migrant background. social housing is also becoming more important in relation to old age poverty. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a very good one. this is a matter of national competence. any transfer of powers through the back door to the eu must therefore be strictly rejected.
in writing. − in my view it is first the duty of a member state – i.e. not the eu’s duty – to ‘take care’ and offer better ‘living standards’ to all of its citizens, including homeless people and materially deprived households with children. by investing in 'social housing programmes', a country defends the fundamental right of its people to live in adequate conditions. secondly, it contributes to a country’s economic growth by generating new investments (e.g. construction, renovation of buildings, efficient energy industry – green jobs) and creating new (local) employment opportunities. i believe that adequate and secure housing should be a precondition in every member state in order to achieve social justice, cohesion and to tackle social exclusion and poverty. as already mentioned, it is first the duty of the member state to ensure the welfare of its people. the eu should interfere in these matters only if member states fail to achieve their set ‘social objectives’. acting in another way would mean breaking the eu agreement as stated in the european union treaty (article 5), meaning acting against the subsidiarity principle.

in writing. the commission has also adopted a proposal for a regulation on the application of the competition rules to the provision of services of general economic interest. i believe that the common competition policy will lead to too much merging of the member countries of the internal market, the banking union and the economic and monetary union as a whole. this has many contra-indications, since the member states have very different starting points in terms of economy, politics and, for example, culture. the problem is that standardization will inevitably lead to inequality, since all participants will be treated equally regardless of performance. i am a supporter of a fair policy and therefore voted against the resolution on this point.
in writing. − in the last years, bearing in mind the financial crisis’ background, it was proved several times that competition is a necessary instrument in the fight against the economical crisis that struck europe. in my opinion, competition is a step to social progress. competition ‘moves’ the engine of one’s economy and ensures the balance and health of the markets. competition on the internal market automatically fosters sme activity, business development, attracts (foreign direct) investments, and also determines a proper price formation that favours and protects the consumer, in other words our citizens.
in writing. − this motion is in favour of a more spending-oriented eu economic policy and against austerity measures in the failing states. in principle, any country that is in debt must also meet these obligations and cannot pass them on to other countries under the guise of a misunderstood 'solidarity'. but this is precisely what is happening in the eu at the moment, and what this proposal would do even more. economic stimulus, in this case financed by well-performing countries such as austria and germany, would be a practical option according to keynes, but keynes also said that the funds for such measures should be saved in times of growth. however, this was not possible because many bankrupt southern countries, such as greece, lived beyond their means for a long time and were admitted to the economic and monetary union despite poor economic data. the continuing financing of the ailing southern countries by the equally highly indebted but still solvent northern euro states is neither reasonable nor fair. the crisis countries should leave the euro, reintroduce their own currency, devalue it and do everything possible to become competitive again. it's their only chance. the eurozone as it stands today is not sustainable. that is why i voted against this motion, which does not reflect reality.
in writing. - i cannot agree with the present resolution, which does not offer a solution to the basic problem and is not without problems in some of its points of view. firstly, the eu must not be given a new opportunity to assume powers it is not entitled to. the european union's massive push for flexible working hours and so on is putting the 5.5 million unemployed young people at risk of being pushed into atypical employment relationships such as permanent internships, part-time work, low-level employment, temporary work, mac-jobs and so on, and thus being consigned to lifelong poverty. the idea, already voiced in the eu, that member states should guarantee all eu citizens under 25 some form of employment within four months of graduating will probably remain a pious wish. in addition, 'some employment' could be understood as a 'more or less' voluntary eu social year. no, youth unemployment is a problem for which each country must find the most appropriate solution.
in writing. − in april 2013, the youth unemployment rate in the european union reached a new record of 23.5%, according to official statistics. in latvia, unfortunately, this figure is even higher than the eu average (28.4% in 2012). i welcomed a number of existing measures to reduce unemployment, such as the growth and jobs pact, with a focus on job creation, especially for young people, as well as the funding allocated to the youth education initiative. however, much remains to be done to reduce youth unemployment rates. i therefore supported the european parliament's resolution on 'european action to combat unemployment', which we drew up in the run-up to the european council on 27 and 28 june 2013 and which contains a number of valuable proposals to be implemented at eu and member state level. there is currently no direct link between what young people learn at university and what a potential employer requires of them. it is therefore essential to make education more competitive by making practical training in companies or public institutions a compulsory part of every study programme in order to help young people adapt to the trends in the labour market. however, the most effective way of preventing unemployment in the long term is to promote sustainable economic growth. it is therefore necessary to support small and medium-sized enterprises, both by helping them to access finance to facilitate job creation and by easing administrative procedures and the tax burden, especially for enterprises that recruit young people.
in writing. - we are currently experiencing one of the worst social crises. in april of this year, almost a quarter of european young people were unemployed. there are major national differences: in austria, youth unemployment is around eight per cent, while in greece it is an incredible 62.5%. if we do not act quickly, we risk losing a whole generation of young europeans. the figures do not merely illustrate the urgency of action. they also show that the austerity policies imposed on the countries in crisis have led to serious social dislocation. long-term investment in education and training programmes and projects such as the european youth guarantee is the only sensible answer. the resolution takes this into account and calls for a significant increase in the funding for the implementation of the youth guarantee in the 2014-2020 multiannual financial framework.
in writing. − tackling youth unemployment in the eu is one of the greatest challenges of our time and must be given priority accordingly; the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the establishment of a european youth employment fund. it is essential to recognise the great potential of europe's young people and to ensure that it can be realised. advanced education and training (in particular dual systems) are a way out of a cycle of poverty and an opportunity to reduce the risk of a 'lost generation'.

the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. i would like to begin by thanking everyone for the constructive cooperation we have had in drawing up this directive between all the political groups, but also with the council and, above all, with the support of the commission, so that we have actually come to a solution here quite quickly, which is supported by all parties. i would like to remind you that water policy is a long-term policy, that it is about making clean water available to our fellow citizens in any form; but water is also the basis for all life on our planet and therefore has a special significance. i would remind you that in 2000 we adopted the water framework directive, which is really a piece of basic legislation, a milestone in global water policy, and which is characterised by three elements. first, it involves all waters. secondly, it operates across borders, i.e. in river basin areas. and third, it wants to achieve good ecological and chemical status for our waters by 2015. and now we have this subsidiary directive which we have worked out together and which sets out specific chemical quality standards so that this good chemical condition can be achieved. unfortunately, research shows that there is still a long way to go in terms of both ecological and chemical good health, especially of surface waters. the environmental quality standards now proposed in this new directive concern 15 new substances. we have already identified 33 priority substances in previous directives from 2003 and 2008 which are considered to be particularly hazardous to the aquatic environment and to humans. now for the next step. in a long process, 15 more substances were defined with stakeholders, for which eqs were established, and for seven existing substances the eqs were revised. the new directive also introduces changes in measurement methods, particularly those which also target biota. so it is not just about providing clean water for people, for our fellow citizens, but also about actually looking at the impact of various chemicals that are classified as hazardous on the natural environment. the compromise package we have forged together is characterized by the following points: we have introduced a new watch list of substances which must be subject to special monitoring in order to classify them later, when more data are available, either as dangerous and with quality standards or as non-hazardous - in other words, special monitoring for substances on this watch list. we start with ten fabrics here, and every year we add one more. secondly, we have added pharmaceutical substances for the first time. this is, as i said, a first big step. there are two hormones and diclofenac, which is an anti-inflammatory drug, which are not already covered by eqs as proposed by the commission, but are placed on a temporary watch list and are being monitored in particular. this will be a particularly interesting area in the future, because unfortunately our waters are increasingly polluted with pharmaceuticals. we have met the council's expectations in terms of the timeframe. the expiry date for the old substances is 2021 and for the new substances is 2027. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's environmental policy is not distorted by the introduction of new substances. if there's any problems here, it's gonna have repercussions on the admission. i think that overall it is a balanced package and i am now counting on the member states to implement it in a timely manner!

in writing. the emissions trading system (ets) involves the auctioning of emission allowances, known as allowances. the basic idea is that certain companies can only emit as much carbon dioxide as they have a right to, or they have to buy a right from a more economical company on an exchange. the eu-wide scheme, introduced in 2005, is designed to reduce emissions from production. the money raised from the sale of rights will be invested in research and development of less polluting technologies. since relatively little has been done in the field of renewable energy since the introduction of the emission allowances, and at the same time there has been an imbalance, with some countries complying with the requirements, but others still having very high co2 emissions, i voted against. it should also be noted that the certificate system is a threat to jobs in europe if only europeans adhere to climate protection standards.

member of the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, once again we have learned all the lessons of the financial crisis, without ever having a short memory. in particular, people who have behaved throughout this crisis, from the beginning and for many years, without any moral or ethical basis, endangering the lives of thousands of citizens and taxpayers around the world. since 2010, with this determination that i had committed to, we have put together this regulatory architecture to bring back transparency where it didn't exist, accountability, rules, and finally, in a way, some morality where it had completely disappeared. all these commitments are in line with what we have decided at the highest level of the global economy the g20 and with the international recommendations of the financial stability board, the icso and the basel committee. all this was reiterated by the 20 leaders of the world's major economic powers a few days ago in st petersburg. i think it is necessary and right that the first item on the agenda of every g20 summit, as in st petersburg, should be to take stock of the implementation of what has been decided over the last five years. in any case, europe is fulfilling the commitments it has made and is almost at the end of the road. that is why, mrs mccarthy, ladies and gentlemen, the text you are debating today, this regulation which i have proposed to you, is an important element on market abuse. it brings transparency and accountability. we had to adapt this european text, which was too weak, because the world has changed - as arlene mccarthy said - trading platforms have multiplied, financial and commodity markets are becoming more integrated, and all new technologies are obviously moving faster than the ability of public authorities to monitor them. finally, more recently, we have discovered what no one, or few, had imagined: these scandals of manipulation of benchmarks, such as libor, which undermine the confidence of both citizens and investors. that is why i have proposed that we strengthen sanctions, with the aim of deterrence, repression and, where necessary, in some cases, imprisonment for those who behave in the most outrageous manner. we have therefore proposed this revision of the market abuse directive in the form of a proposal for a regulation to go faster. i am very pleased that the council adopted a political agreement with parliament on this draft regulation on 26 june and i would like to express my sincere thanks to arlene mccarthy, but also to sharon bowles, to the various fictitious rapporteurs, mrs pietikäinen, mr klinz, mr giegold and mrs swinburne. your work has also enabled us to improve, as is often the case, existing legislation, including my own proposal. the regulation takes account of the developments on the financial markets which i have just mentioned, in particular the new trading platforms, mtfs and otfs, over-the-counter transactions, co2 emission allowances. it adapts our framework to the new technologies of high frequency trading as much as possible and ensures that new forms of market abuse made possible by these new technologies are clearly prohibited. finally, and this is important to me, the regulation deals with the volatility and financialization of commodity markets, which are also subject to too much manipulation. i am therefore very pleased that this regulatory framework has been extended to cover market abuse in both commodity and derivatives markets. this is a very significant change, as is the very last response i proposed to you - and you supported it - to the libor scandal and the manipulation of benchmarks, which will be the subject of a new, extremely strict regulatory framework that i will propose, together with the european commission, next week. dissuasion is an essential element in the fight against abuse. it involves the detection of abuse, severe sanctions and, where necessary, prison sentences. the regulation gives the competent authorities the necessary powers to detect abuses and conduct investigations, while naturally respecting the very wide diversity of national legal systems and the fundamental rights of citizens. i would like to thank parliament for supporting this increase in administrative sanctions. to give just one example, ladies and gentlemen, the possibility of imposing fines of up to 15% of turnover is a very clear signal that such market abuse and manipulation is unacceptable and will no longer be tolerated. i know that parliament would have wished to go further. i can understand that. that is why we have included a clause for revision, which will probably allow us to come back to this point. finally, a word on the directive on criminal sanctions for market abuse, which is part of this package of proposals. i know that parliament wants to make progress in the trilogues on this text as well. that is also my concern and i hope that we can make significant progress with the lithuanian presidency to complete this text, which is part of the package, with mif 2 and the directive on criminal sanctions that i have just mentioned. these are two important texts and so we have a lot of work to do together on this subject in the coming days and weeks.
draft opinion of the consultative committee on the environment, public health and food safety. - mr president, i have to say something. the european union has created a market-based instrument in its fight against climate change - the european emissions trading system. and this system is 80% covered by the mifid directive. the regulation under discussion here also incorporates the remaining 20%. it therefore concerns the unregulated spot and primary markets. the ets has, of course, various specific features. the disclosure requirements which in other markets are primarily for issuers are here imposed on market participants. the issuers are the states, or in the third period, the commission. these disclosure obligations are of course intended to apply only to those market participants which have an influence on price formation. the ets market is structured in such a way that approximately 7% of the participants are responsible for 80% of emissions and approximately half of the allowances are used by, say, 20 companies. it is therefore sensible to introduce special rules here, but it is of course important that we also sanction market abuse accordingly so that this market can function properly.

i have to say, madam president, one of the main achievements of the lisbon treaty is the creation of an area of freedom, security and justice, which is equivalent to the objectives of completing economic and monetary union and the internal market. it was therefore only logical to subject this area to the co-decision procedure. this is a fundamental consideration which we must bear in mind when we discuss today the amendment of council regulation no 539/2001. in this context, facilitating access to visas is therefore no longer in the national interest. a common area of freedom, security and justice requires a community strategy and thus the cooperation of the council, parliament and the commission. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval. it would therefore be in everyone's interest to strengthen this european aspect, and above all in the interest of the european parliament. the rapporteur, whom i greatly appreciate for his factual work and who has also done a great deal of positive work in the context of this report, has unfortunately ended up taking the opposite position and has not taken this european perspective as seriously as he should have. that is why we must reject his report, because we all hope that we can bring the rights of the european parliament back into this debate in a second reading!
i have to say, madam president, when the european parliament supported this visa exemption for south-eastern european countries in 2010, it was a very deliberate and sensible decision. but if we now find that the asylum applications from this region are suddenly increasing to the extent that they are, that some 16% of the asylum applications are already coming from south-eastern europe - germany, sweden and switzerland in particular are affected - then we have to react here. i therefore strongly support the fact that measures are now being taken to prevent the paralysis of the asylum system by a flood of applications which are clearly unfounded. the most important measure - and i consider it wise and necessary - to combat the abuse of asylum is to adopt a safeguard clause when there is a significant and sudden increase in irregular stayers or asylum seekers who make an application for asylum without any apparent justification, or cases where return agreements are not implemented. this is a very good proposal and it will help to ensure that the asylum system is not paralysed but that asylum procedures are expedited. that's the goal behind it. and secondly, i welcome the introduction of the reciprocity mechanism. this will certainly lead to greater solidarity among the member states.
the commission has already made a number of proposals. my colleague from the greens, tatjana ždanoka, has already said that we greens will not support this motion because we do not support this right of suspension and we believe that there is a real need for parliamentary involvement in the full form guaranteed by the treaty of lisbon. as rapporteur for kosovo, i would also like to point out that the kosovars are the only people in the balkans who are not yet allowed to travel freely at all. freedom of movement is one of the achievements of the enlargement process. but i must also make a comment on mr obermayr, the austrian liberal colleague who spoke here: you said that hundreds of buses come and then return empty. well, of course. when buses come, they bring people. and freedom of movement means that people can stay in austria and elsewhere and watch it there, visit relatives, etc. they're not going back with the people. your argument is far from sound.
i have to say, madam president, even if the honourable member, mr weidenholzer, and mrs lunacek do not want to admit it, tens of thousands of third country nationals have been abusing both the eu asylum system and the eu visa system in recent years. the commission has also proposed a safeguard clause to suspend visa-free travel if illegal immigration increases. and this clause is necessary! the member states must exercise their discretion. if there is an acute problem, we cannot wait for the commission to take a long decision on this proposal. the visa requirement must be adapted to the changing immigration situation in a rapid and flexible manner. if we know this from the past from good examples or bad examples illegals once in the country, subsequent deportation is difficult if not impossible. in writing. − on paper, the rights of the defence and the right to a fair trial (which are enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights and the european convention for the protection of human rights) are to be strengthened. the european union has a duty to ensure that the rights of the citizens of the union are respected and that the rights of the citizens of the union are respected. the european parliament has been a very active participant in the debate on the future of the european union, and it has been a very active participant in the debate on the future of the european union. the eu must abandon its us subordination and finally stand up for human and fundamental values. until it does so, this directive is a worthless piece of paper. i have therefore rejected the report.
in writing. - without mortgage loans, most people would not be able to afford housing. this is why this form of credit is of great economic importance. and of course, the financial and economic crisis that has been going on since 2008 is also having an impact on this area. mortgage loans are usually taken out in one's own country. crossborder activities are the exception in this area. the eu wants to create an internal market for mortgage loans that is stable, resilient, efficient and open to competition. i think some of the approaches to the project are quite desirable. i think that the current structure of the community is not very sensible, especially in view of the bursting of the housing bubble, and is more likely to create new bureaucratic obstacles and credit taxation or even credit shortages. in the end, a local banker is more likely to grant a loan than a cross-border financial institution. i have therefore rejected the report.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud. many people get access to housing through a loan. on the other hand, the mortgage lending market, with its sometimes irresponsible lending practices, has contributed to one of the biggest financial and economic crises. i therefore believe that regulation in this area is urgently needed and welcome this bill as a first step towards fairer, more inclusive and more responsible lending. the european parliament's proposals are clearly aimed at improving consumer protection: for example, more flexibility on early repayment, provisions on responsible lending, some protection against risks associated with foreign currency loans and a cooling-off period for consumers were proposed. in future, credit institutions will be required to provide consumers with comprehensive information and to comply with certain minimum standards, such as the prohibition of misleading advertising.
in writing. − the trading of inside information allows for targeted manipulation of financial and stock markets. this allows a few insiders to enrich themselves at the expense of the general public and at the same time undermines the stability of financial markets. these unfair practices must be put to a legal halt. in addition to the existing mifid directive, which covers insider dealing in many areas, it was now necessary to close further loopholes by recasting the regulation of the european parliament and of the council on insider dealing and market manipulation (market abuse). the new system will also cover emission allowances. i believe that this is a major contribution to the proper functioning of the markets and to the prevention of market abuse, which is why i voted in favour of the proposal for a regulation.
in writing. − a level playing field is essential for the functioning of the internal market. equally important is investor protection. the new regulation aims to prevent, or at least make more difficult, insider trading and market manipulation. it also extends the legal framework to all financial instruments, including carbon credits. as reducing co2 emissions is a major objective for many eu member states, a functioning emissions trading market must be ensured. otherwise, dumping prices could result, which would permanently render the idea of co2 emission allowances absurd and undermine investment in lower-emission technology developments. this is in contrast to a future-oriented industrial policy which takes environmental protection more seriously. i therefore voted in favour of the legislative resolution.
in writing. - exactly five years ago, the lehman brothers collapse triggered the financial crisis. the libor manipulation scandal revealed a little over a year ago that not much has changed in financial markets in terms of work ethic and work ethics. that is why i am pleased that this report is the first to define insider dealing at european level and to extend the concept of market manipulation to include collusion and price fixing in such important areas as exchange rate markets and energy and oil and gas commodity markets. by introducing minimum penalties and the fact that attempted manipulation is already punishable, we are giving regulators and supervisors greater leverage against companies that engage in market manipulation. finally, the explicit protection of so-called whistleblowers ensures that persons who help to uncover such scandals do not have to fear retaliation from the employer. i therefore voted in favour of the present bill.
in writing. − all the eu's energy policy considerations and actions, such as privatisation and liberalisation of the energy market, have so far failed to deliver the promised cost reductions for consumers. the internal energy market is a major potential for vat fraud. in germany alone, it is estimated that each kilowatt hour of electricity is resold seven to eight times before it reaches the customer. with a market volume for electricity and gas trading of several hundred billion euros, vat fraud could be widespread here, apart from the fact that costs naturally increase with each further purchase and sale. the gaps in energy trading must be closed and the rules changed so that the customer actually has a chance to benefit from lower prices on the wholesale market. so far, however, only increases have been passed on, not reductions. i consider the present proposal to be immature in this respect and therefore reject it.
in writing. − the assessment of the baseline situation is correct in the legislative proposal: reducing the eu's energy consumption is of far-reaching importance. it is also foreseeable that the eu's rather ambitious target of reducing overall energy consumption by 20% by 2020 will not be achieved under the current trend. but i think it is unreasonable to conclude from these circumstances that the state (eu and member state) is now a better investor than the private sector. the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the efficiency of the energy sector. the use of the cohesion fund often shows an unreasonable allocation of funds or even over-investment, which is not due to necessity but is purely a means of using up the financial quotas allocated to the national authorities. a money pitcher often lacks the ability to make a wise selection in identifying sensible investments, and only billions are sunk accordingly. the task of policy is to provide the right incentives for industry and citizens to make these investments. i therefore voted against this legislative resolution.
in writing. the eu is the world's largest employer of translators. the translation effort required for 24 official languages is high, but necessary, since this multilingualism allows citizens to exercise their right to democratic control. translations thus make a significant contribution to the openness and transparency of the eu institutions towards their citizens. the quality is also good. unfortunately, there are a number of problems, in particular late cancellation for use, which have caused unnecessary costs of around eur 15 million over the last three years. the legislative proposal now presented a number of practical measures to reduce such types of waste in day-to-day operations. i have therefore agreed to the proposal, since it will increase the efficiency of the necessary translation services while maintaining quality.
in writing. − gambling, especially online gambling, is a growing industry within the eu. the legislative proposal aims primarily to combat illegal gambling, to increase the protection and information of vulnerable groups on online gambling and to improve measures to combat illegal gambling. indeed, it is right to try to combat the growing problem of illegal gambling - and a number of proposals are promising. the proposal to finance sports from the state's gambling revenues and the catalogue of measures against collusion are also to be welcomed. the eu framework is justified in that the internet is a spaceless medium and a vote is best achieved at eu level. however, the voices for more information and deterrence of vulnerable groups are unreliable or at least ineffective in practice - think of tobacco products. the fact that online gambling is being strengthened by a broader legal framework could even increase its growth and support - and therefore indirectly, unfortunately, illegal gambling, despite all the measures taken to combat it. the number of addicts could increase and the evidence on the interaction between the growth of gambling and the acute economic crisis is also worrying. in short, the eu measure could be a boomerang. i have therefore decided to abstain.
in writing. - i am particularly concerned about the repeal or amendment of article 19, which recommends that the commission impose network blocks. as the european parliament, we should be advocating a free and democratic internet and not measures that restrict fundamental rights. by imposing internet bans, the policy avoids its duty to act against proven illegal content. blocklists are not enough because they are easy to circumvent and only encourage looking the other way. the illegal activities of some website operators are not prevented by a visual barrier, but only covered. barriers create an opaque and non-transparent field in which industry is empowered to enforce private law. as 'lawmakers', we should not delegate this right to industry. at the same time, the scope of application can be extended at any time, as examples from the past show. so i am against internet blocking and instead i am calling for an effective fight against illegal sites instead of a symbol policy that does not work.

ombudsman. − mr president, before i begin my remarks, may i just, with great pleasure, welcome you back. i am delighted to see that you are in very good health and wish you very well. this is obviously a moment replete with some degree of emotion for me. i would like to thank parliament for the opportunity to address you on the subject of my annual report for the year 2012. to begin with i would like to express my profound thanks to your rapporteur, mr salavrakos, for his thorough and insightful report on the ombudsman’s activities and my gratitude to the committee on petitions for serving as a valuable source of inspiration and support to the ombudsman throughout my decade in office. i particularly wish to record my gratitude to mr salavrakos for the remarks on a personal level that he has just made. they touched me deeply. in 2012, over 22 000 citizens were directly helped by the ombudsman. of these, around 19 000 received advice through the interactive guide on my website. we should not underestimate how important it is for citizens to be guided to the most appropriate complaint-handling body from the outset and to be spared the frustrations and delays associated with having to identify the right institution on their own. in 2012 i also received a total of 2 442 complaints from citizens, enterprises, ngos, associations and others. the 465 inquiries opened in 2012 represent an increase of 18 % compared to the previous year. this again follows a similar increase of 18 % in 2011. the trend towards more people turning to the european ombudsman for the right reasons is confirmed by the continued fall in the number of complaints received that are outside the mandate. in 2012 the number of such complaints stood at 1 720, which is the lowest in ten years. i attribute this success, which this body had persistently been asking me for, to the interactive guide that i mentioned earlier. in 2012, 390 inquiries were closed. in 89 cases, the institution concerned settled the matter, agreed to a friendly solution or accepted a draft recommendation. most of the other cases were closed with a finding either of no maladministration or that no further inquiries were needed. i found maladministration in 56 cases. the institutions accepted a draft recommendation either in part or in full in nine of these while the other 47 were closed with critical remarks. in 30 cases i made further remarks to help improve future performance. in 2012 we were able for the first time to provide a concrete answer to the question of how well the institutions cooperate with the european ombudsman in seeking to improve their performance. in two publications produced last year, the follow-up study to critical and further remarks and a new compliance report, we found that in 82 % of cases the eu institutions complied with the ombudsman’s suggestions. i will take advantage of vice-president reding’s presence, who i had not acknowledged when i thanked her for being here, to also note that the degree of compliance for the commission last year stood at exactly 82 %. helping to ensure the highest standards of behaviour in the institutions constitutes a key element of the ombudsman’s mission. during 2012, following a public consultation, we formulated and published a set of public service principles. the five principles represent a succinct statement of what citizens and civil servants alike expect of the eu civil service. they are: (1) commitment to the european union and its citizens (2) integrity (3) objectivity (4) respect for others and (5) transparency. these principles take account of best practice in the member states and among other things should help civil servants to understand and apply correctly the plethora of codes and regulations governing their activities. since i will be retiring at the end of this month, i wish also to use this opportunity to provide you with a short overview of what i think have been the notable achievements and important experiences of the institution which you elected me to lead three times over the past decade. in basic numbers, over the last ten and a half years the european ombudsman dealt with more than 30 000 complaints and opened almost 3 500 in-depth investigations into alleged maladministration by the eu institutions. during the same period the eu administration has become more transparent, more citizen-friendly and more service-minded. i am convinced that the independent and impartial work of the ombudsman has contributed to this notable progress towards an administration culture of service to citizens. we have achieved tangible results in many fields especially as regards transparency, ethical issues such as conflicts of interest and citizens’ rights. since the lisbon treaty entered into force in 2009 and the charter of fundamental rights became legally binding, the ombudsman has become increasingly active in the area of citizens’ rights in relation, for example, to the european citizens’ initiative, the institutions’ obligation to conduct an open and regular dialogue with civil society and other ways of increased citizen participation including public consultations. the ombudsman has also participated in multiple ways in decision-making and opinion-forming at the european level and in strengthening cooperation with the european network of ombudsmen. important parts of my work have involved adapting the ombudsman’s office to take account of enlargement, the reform of the ombudsman statute, advising on the establishment of the ombudsman institution in turkey, agreeing the memorandum of understanding with the european data protection supervisor in the european investment bank, enhancing the ombudsman's role in relation to the protection of human and fundamental rights, strengthening the european network of ombudsmen and, not least, providing parliament with information and recommendations in a number of fields. promoting an administrative culture of service to citizens requires a moral investment on the part of the ombudsman and on the part of parliament and the other institutions and bodies of the union. it asks of the ombudsman to be proactive, to be imaginative and to be creative in thinking of ways to bring about changes in the mindset of the institutions. above all, however, promoting a culture of service demands of the ombudsman institution the intellectual commitment and administrative capacity to adopt citizen-focused strategies geared to the maintenance and observance of the highest ethical standards. such attributes constitute the necessary foundation on which to build the moral and political capital that is needed to make it possible for the ombudsman to live up to the added responsibilities and heavy expectations associated with being viewed as an important institutional counterweight to executive power, capable of speaking truth to power and endowed with moral authority allowing him or her to contribute substantively to the deepening of the rule of law and to the enhancement of the quality of democracy within the european union. it is important to acknowledge that little progress would have been possible without the good cooperation of the leadership and staff of the eu institutions. meaningfully, creatively and proactively engaging in a regular and structured dialogue with the institutions, for which the ombudsman serves as an external mechanism of control, constitutes a central element of my deeply held view that the ombudsman should not be regarded as an institutional expression of a culture of blame, which tends to breed a defensive mentality in the institutions and staff. rather, my objective has been proactively to promote a culture of service to citizens and of active respect for their rights. with respect to the commission, i wish here to acknowledge the support of successive commissioners for administration, international relations and fundamental rights. we have also built an excellent framework of cooperation with the european investment bank. a further source of satisfaction is that the agencies of the eu have in their overwhelming majority cooperated fully with me in promoting the principles of a culture of service in their relations with citizens. i again profit from the presence of ms reding to also underline the way in which she, from her new portfolio – that is extremely important for us – has been supportive of the ombudsman over the past few years and i want to thank her for that. finally, i would like to acknowledge the central role of parliament in general, and its committee on petitions in particular, in providing generous support to the ombudsman institution. parliament has ensured that the ombudsman has the budgetary and human resources needed to work effectively and has provided firm political support for the ombudsman’s efforts to achieve progress and good administration in the defence of citizens’ rights. this has been a collaborative endeavour which i believe has achieved notably good results for citizens. i will conclude with some reflections on the challenges for the future. parliament has, in its collective wisdom, elected ms emily o’reilly as my successor. as the outgoing irish ombudsman, ms o’reilly comes well prepared for the tasks lying ahead. during her 10 years in office in ireland, she distinguished herself on both the domestic and international fronts. domestically, she presided over the major enlargement and renovation of her institution and over the subsequent enhancement of its moral authority and its political weight. internationally, she played a central role in the growth and development of both the british and irish ombudsmen association and the european network of ombudsmen as vibrant and more professional groups. last, but certainly not least, as the very first female european ombudsman, she brings to her task the ingenuity, emotional intelligence and intuition especially associated with her gender. as such, she comes superbly prepared for the challenges facing her institution. one such challenge is the economic situation which both the citizens whom we serve and the institutions we are tasked to help have to face, in all likelihood, for quite some time. another challenge will be to cope with and adjust to technological change, environmental, economic and financial problems, increasing but also ageing populations, and many others including migration. these challenges are leaving their deep imprint on the evolving relationship between the eu and its citizens. in turn, the expectations which citizens hold of the eu that serves them are a function of two central parameters: the problems they face, and the tools they have at their disposal in order to make their demands known. the challenge for the european ombudsman is to be both responsive to the changing needs and demands of citizens and, at the same time, be aware of the pressures and constraints that the institutions face. i wish my successor well and i thank you all for your attention and for your support for the past 10 years, and for the honour that you have bestowed upon me three times to serve you. (applause)

salavrakos and the committee on petitions for the excellent report on the activities of the european ombudsman in 2012. this report is important because it shows us how the controller of the controller views the way that this very citizen-centred work has been put in place. this work has been put in place because you, mr. diamandouros, over all this time, have first of all built up an institution and then led it. this required patience, professionalism and wisdom. you had all three of them, and i think that parliament was very wise three times to give you the responsibility of leading this institution. mr salavrakos' report also looks back and highlights what has been achieved in recent years. this includes constant efforts to deepen the dialogue with citizens, and i hear with great pleasure that citizens increasingly know what the responsibility of the ombudsman entails, so this institution is becoming a real fact of life for citizens. that recognition takes time to build and you have managed to do just that a real achievement. you have also managed, by deepening the dialogue not only with citizens but also with the institutions and civil society, to strengthen the rapporteur. mr president, i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. it is not so long ago that we in this house not only discussed the brussels i regulation but also, as european legislators, very constructively participated in its revision. since 12 december 2012, we have now signed the recast of the regulation on jurisdiction and the recognition and enforcement of judgments in civil and commercial matters. there are many improvements: this is clearly an added value for the citizens of europe. the exequatur procedure, for example, has been abolished and it will be easier to carry out such executions in the future. however, the commission has chosen the recasting technique in this project and has accordingly omitted some aspects in this procedure which are very important in my view and in the view of the legal affairs committee. the procedure did not cover important aspects relevant to employment law. the important link between jurisdiction in labour matters and the legal system applicable to employment contracts has not been sufficiently taken into account. the workplace has become more transnational and, above all, more rigid. this is proved by spectacular european court cases - i call them torline, but also viking - to which i think we must react. there is a need for european action. the report is based on the principle that the existing labour law provisions of the member states must be protected against being undermined by the competent courts of other member states, or in other words, forum shopping must be prevented. it is necessary to ensure that the courts of a member state have jurisdiction where the labour law of that state is applicable. the place of jurisdiction should be the member state whose law is now applicable. this principle should apply to industrial action and employment contracts. we point out in the report that one of the fundamental principles of private international law is to protect the weaker party, and that often includes people who are employed or involved in industrial action. the european parliament believes that the commission should look at labour law issues in a more in-depth way than it did during the recast to brussels i. the rights and obligations of trade unions in industrial action now vary considerably from one member state to another. what is constitutionally protected in one country may even be illegal in another. i therefore propose that the provisions of the brussels i regulation be brought into line with those of the rome ii regulation on the law applicable to non-contractual obligations. the place of jurisdiction in relation to industrial action should be the place where the industrial action is or has been taking place. the commission, the report says, should pay particular attention to this issue. the commission should also pay more attention to individual employment contracts. the brussels i regulation already contains specific provisions for the protection of workers and for the protection of consumers and insured persons. the reserve criterion of the establishment where the worker was employed often leads to problems in the field of international transport. often there is no real link between the establishment and the daily work. it is difficult to determine from where the employee has been working. a company could be registered in one member state, the means of transport in another. the management is then established in a member state c and the worker may be resident in a member state d. you see, these are all cases which can happen and which require the commission to pay more attention to these issues and in particular to the principle of protecting the weaker party.

i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. the elimination of the large number of bilateral investment agreements between the eu member states and china is a sensible move. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rules on the protection of investors are respected. this means that the same law should apply to all member states. the eu's economic superiority - still present - and the good negotiating position it enjoys should not, however, lead to any temptation to be careless or hasty. in addition to the mandatory, self-evident transparency and fairness of the negotiations, it is important to observe certain rules of the game. for example, public services must be excluded from the negotiations, restrictions must also be imposed in sectors where there is a legitimate public interest, and of course - very important and already mentioned today - we want to ensure that important european social, environmental and data protection standards are respected. chinese investment is fine and dandy, but certainly not with social and environmental dumping in europe!

a bilateral investment agreement between the eu and china would be of great importance. the agreement would thus apply to the entire eu area and replace the existing bilateral agreements between a total of 26 eu member states. the effect of such an agreement should be to increase investment in the eu and also in china significantly. in 2011, these investments were around 2% by the eu and 0,4% by china. the agreement will open up access to a highly attractive and vast chinese consumer market, which could benefit many european investors. the main focus is on foreign direct investment, which is of particular interest to the eu. to achieve this, the agreement aims to level off market access restrictions on the one hand and the unequal competition between chinese and european investors on the other. to cover the latter in a comprehensive way, the agreement should include binding clauses on social and environmental standards, the protection of european public services, intellectual property rights and data protection. finally, in addition to the above, the agreement aims to provide greater transparency, legal certainty and fair treatment for eu investors.

in writing. the use of heavy metals such as cadmium and mercury in production has historically been of great economic importance. unfortunately, this has also had negative effects on people and the environment. in recent years, therefore, far-reaching legislative measures have been adopted to restrict the use of heavy metals. this has been successful: in my home country, austria, there is evidence of a reduction in the cadmium and mercury deposits in the ground. the revision of the directive to be adopted today is a logical consequence of developments in recent years: the placing on the market of batteries and accumulators containing cadmium was already prohibited in 2006. the existing exemption for cordless power tools is also abolished. it is important that the prohibition as of 31 december 2016 is set in such a way that the economic operators concerned have sufficient time to be able to introduce the relevant substitute technologies. i am also particularly pleased that we have taken the opportunity to repeal another outdated exception: mercury must no longer be contained in button cells. this is particularly important because button cells are often not disposed of via the special waste and are therefore particularly harmful to the environment.

in writing. - the successes of the european education system over the last 250 years have been based in particular on the evolution of successful systems. this means that those systems which had proved most successful were adopted by other states. this approach is based on the fact that there were no centralised guidelines from a planning department in brussels. while it is welcome that there is some exchange of such good practice through a central body, pisa and co. are enough incentives for member states to reflect on their current situation and to make improvements where necessary. such improvements should then be based on good copying or the principle of invention and evolution mentioned above. the report, on the other hand, seeks to increase regional influence through the use of brussels guidelines, by allowing the ministries of culture to be given certain guidelines in the field of education and curriculum. this is absurd in the light of the points raised so far. not only are people not getting any smarter, it's undermining the evolutionary idea of successful system exchange. we have already seen through the bologna process the problems that have resulted from standardised university-level guidelines. i therefore rejected the report.

in writing. − drug precursors are substances which are legal and used for the production of drugs. for example, acetic acid is used in the manufacture of heroin. some drug precursors are listed as controlled substances in the existing regulation, which are divided into three categories: category 1 is subject to strict export, import and transit formalities, while category 3 scheduled substances are subject to certain formalities only if exported to certain countries. the problem is with medicines containing ephedrine and pseudoephedrine, which have been excluded from the scope of application to date. however, such medicinal products are not covered by the category of controlled substances and are subject to special rules. i voted for the report because it is essential to crack down on drug trafficking. this includes the trade in substances from which drugs can be made. the eu must ensure that it does not become the norm to set up drug laboratories in apartments, houses and storage rooms with relative ease. the more difficult it is to obtain the substances needed to make drugs, the more difficult it is to obtain drugs.
in writing. the amendment to the regulation is intended to combat more effectively the illicit trade in chemical precursors for the production of drugs, in particular the substance acetane hydride used in the manufacture of heroin. the adaptation of the directive is important because the large quantities of this chemical produced and traded are very difficult to control, and although three quarters of seizures are made in the eu, this represents only a fraction of the quantity that disappears each year. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. i was able to accept the request without any reservations, not least because these databases have been subject to extensive data protection provisions.
in writing. − it is essential that the regulation laying down rules for the control of trade in drug precursors between the community and third countries functions properly in order to be able to take proactive action against drug production and trafficking. it is sensible and desirable to include medicinal products which can be used to manufacture drugs in the scope of the regulation.
in writing. − drug precursors are chemicals that can be used to produce narcotics. these include substances which, although not addictive, can be converted into a narcotic (e.g. ephedrine, lysergic acid). precursors in the broad sense include other chemical substances such as acids, bases and organic solvents. they are suitable for the manufacture of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, but are not incorporated in the narcotic itself. since only small doses of drug precursors are needed to produce hard drugs, careful handling and strict control of these substances is essential. since it would be too expensive to produce these substances themselves, which are usually produced in large quantities at great industrial cost, mechanisms need to be created, such as the establishment of an eu-wide database of substances concerned. that is why i voted for the report.
in writing. − intensive monitoring of drug precursors is an important contribution to the fight against drug addiction and crime. in particular, acetic anhydride (the raw material for heroin) needs to be closely monitored to avoid illicit processing. the european union can take decisive steps to make it less attractive as a location for drug production.
in writing. − the intelligent use of technology is certainly one way of reducing costs. the new e-justice portal is also welcome, which can provide a great deal of information, provided that open questions can be resolved and that the database is maintained on an ongoing basis. to some extent, this may also result in an increase in citizen services. but only as long as people are not forced to be happy. it is all too easy to pass the cost on to the recipient. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of the euro against counterfeiting. i believe that these points have not been taken into account sufficiently to justify my unreserved support for the present action plan.
